title: Without the Jargon: Who Approves What
markdown:
Open Executive is organized like a real company: a set of departments, each with a person who can act as its head, and a clear rule for who is allowed to sign off on what. When a piece of work needs a human's approval, the system doesn't guess from job titles — it looks for the person who carries the matching permission.

### Permissions are tags, not titles

Every person on the roster carries one or more approval tags describing what they are cleared to approve:

- **Approve money under $10k** — the bookkeeper or operations-finance person
- **Approve money under $2k** — anyone with a corporate card
- **Sign off on hires** — the principal or the HR head
- **Onboard a new vendor** — whoever owns that area
- **Speak for the board** — the board-communications owner
- **Extend customer credit** — the head of sales or customer success
- **Anyone, anything** — the principal, the final stop

### How a proposal finds its person

When the system drafts something that needs a signature — a new vendor, a contractor hire, a customer-facing release — it parks the draft and looks for someone who holds the matching tag. It routes the proposal to that person and waits; nothing is sent until they approve. If no one carries the right tag, the proposal falls back to the principal. The principal is always the last resort and the final say.

### Just you

If you use Open Executive just for yourself (solo mode) — whether you run your own business, lead a function inside a bigger company, or work independently — it works for you alone. Departments become **areas** — a way to group your goals — and every proposal comes to you. Your manager, your team, your clients and your board are still real people: the Executive helps you work with them (prepping a review, an update, a hard conversation), but it never posts to a team room or broadcasts, and never messages anyone you haven't asked it to. Tell it a new goal — "I want 20 paying clients by December" — and it starts tracking it under the right area, adding the area if you don't have one yet. When you promise something by a date ("I'll send the proposal by Friday"), it keeps track, reminds you when it's due, and lists it under **Due soon** on your Briefing until you mark it done.
